strengths: Originality and significance: The unified target–helper formulation offers useful understanding of auxiliary optimization. Its main contribution is connecting Hessian similarity to savings in expensive target-gradient calls, building on SVRG, momentum variance reduction, and MIME. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b08/review-experiment-pae_mwl5/call-89dc714853254552816077faa03d956f/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Soundness of the core mechanism: Equation (3) gives a simple correction whose deterministic gradient error is bounded by δ times the distance from the snapshot. This explains why auxiliary functions can help despite large gradient offsets or different minimizers. The distinction between Hessian similarity and gradient bias is valuable.

Empirical merits: The quadratic experiments isolate bias and similarity, while MNIST, CIFAR, and logistic-regression experiments provide evidence of useful behavior beyond the toy setting. Including the matched-total-work SGDm baseline in Section 6.3 is helpful.

Presentation, reproducibility, and limitations: The derivation, pseudocode, appendices, and code link support understanding and implementation. The authors appropriately acknowledge that Hessian similarity need not hold for the proposed deep-learning applications and that constructing correlated estimators remains unresolved. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Theorems 4.6/C.10 are false with the printed step size. Take f(x)=x²/2, h(x)=0, x₀=1, K=2, L=δ=1, and exact gradients and initialization. For sufficiently large T, the prescribed step size is η=1/√(66T), and AuxMVR gives x_t=(1−2η)x_{t−1}. The reported average squared gradient is therefore Θ(T⁻¹ᐟ²), whereas the theorem claims O(T⁻¹). The final step-size cap omits the helper-variance dependence; correcting the theorem and reconciling its proof are necessary before relying on Corollary 4.7.

Soundness of the decentralized extension: Appendix C.4 updates momentum only for sampled helpers but transfers the single-helper momentum analysis without addressing stale local states. Lemma C.8 does not automatically hold when a helper misses rounds. With S=1 and many helpers, even identical helpers h_i=0 can retain outdated momentum for long periods, contradicting a participation-independent extension of the stated rate. The update protocol and error recursion need revision. Theorem C.15 also omits the stronger Assumption 4.5 required by the MVR analysis.

Connection between theory and experiments: Section 6 states that K=1 recovers SGDm. This holds for Algorithm 4 but generally not for the analyzed Algorithm 3. Appendix C.2.1 explicitly says that no similarity-dependent benefit was proved for Algorithm 4. The manuscript must identify the variant used in each experiment and establish which findings validate the analyzed method. AuxMVR itself receives no empirical evaluation.

Significance of the practical acceleration claims: Target-oracle savings require additional helper work, potentially with K growing as σ_h²/ε. The experiments provide no runtime or measured oracle-cost comparison, and a smaller coreset does not automatically make an individual minibatch gradient cheaper. Section 6.3 largely matches the total-work baseline and asserts negligible overhead without measurements. This supports a target-access tradeoff more clearly than a demonstrated training-speed advantage.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript does not specify repeat counts or explain the shaded uncertainty regions. CIFAR architecture details and optimization settings, fine-tuning schedules, and step-size search ranges are incomplete. These omissions, together with the algorithm ambiguity, make the reported comparisons difficult to reproduce and their variability difficult to assess.
